extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, in-house counsel, IP managers and businesses with European patent portfolios
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guide to the unitary patent and Unified Patent Court (UPC), explaining jurisdiction, opt-out rules, court structure, procedures, language, timing, remedies and costs for litigating or managing European patents under the new system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unitary patent scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The unitary patent will provide patent protection in all participating states with a single patent registration, without the need for national validation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unitary patents supplement the existing patent system and coexist with national patents and classic European patents; once converted to unitary effect, the proprietor pays a recurring fee to the EPO and cannot drop certain country designations over the lifetime of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: UPC exclusive jurisdiction (scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC will have exclusive jurisdiction for disputes relating to infringement and validity of unitary patents and classic European patents for participating member states which have not been opted out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The UPC has no competence over national patents. During the transitional period there will be dual jurisdiction for classic EPs not opted out; after transition, non-opted classic EPs become subject to UPC exclusivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and transitional periods
rubrics_metrics.description: The system is expected to become operational on 1 June 2023; transitional measures (early unitary effect requests and delay requests to grant) took effect on 1 January 2023; the sunrise period (opt-out filing window start) is planned to start on 1 March 2023. The transitional opt-out period is seven years, possibly extendable to 14 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The UPC will only enter into force three months after Germany deposits its ratification. Dates are subject to change; proprietors should monitor ratification steps and the UPC timetable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opt-out availability for classic European patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Proprietors of classic European patents may opt out from UPC jurisdiction during the transitional period; an opt-out renders the UPC without jurisdiction over that EP and the patent remains subject to national courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opt-outs are only for classic European patents (not unitary patents) and normally remain in force for the life of the European patent unless withdrawn by the proprietor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opt-out application requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: An opt-out application must be signed (not just registered) by all proprietors of the patent for all EPC states for which the EP is granted or designated; if an SPC has been granted, the SPC proprietor (if different) must also sign, unless the SPC application is pending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensees do not have the right to opt out unless the licence agreement expressly provides that right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect and duration of opt-out
rubrics_metrics.description: Once notified and registered, an opt-out takes effect for the European patent for all participating member states where the patent has been validated, and normally remains in force for the lifetime of the European patent unless the proprietor withdraws it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An opt-out protects the EP from UPC jurisdiction across participating states; proprietors should consider global portfolio strategy before opting out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal of opt-out
rubrics_metrics.description: An opt-out may be withdrawn at any time provided no proceedings regarding that European patent, European patent application or SPC have been commenced in the national courts; an opt-out can only be withdrawn once, and once withdrawn the patent cannot be opted out again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withdrawal is constrained: if national proceedings have started, withdrawal is not permitted; strategic implications for enforcement and validity challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unitary patent prosecution and conversion timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The prosecution of a unitary patent does not differ from classic European patents and is via the EPO; within one month of grant, the applicant can decide to convert the patent into a unitary patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once unitary effect is established, the proprietor no longer needs to validate nationally and must pay recurring EPO fees; conversion is a positive decision by the applicant shortly after grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unitary patent irrevocability of country designations
rubrics_metrics.description: Once unitary effect is established, it will no longer be possible to drop certain country designations over the lifetime of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This permanent territorial effect should be considered before opting for unitary effect, as it limits future territorial adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical participation and ratification requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To be covered by the unitary patent, a member state must be participating in the enhanced cooperation and must have ratified the UPCA when the unitary patent is registered; 25 EU member states participate in enhanced cooperation, with an initial set of ratifiers to operate at launch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A state's participation depends on both enhanced cooperation membership and formal ratification; the list of participating states may change as further ratifications occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: SPCs based on unitary patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplementary Protection Certificates (SPCs) based on unitary patents are possible; an SPC based on a unitary patent cannot be opted out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission has consulted on a proposed unitary SPC and unified procedure for national SPCs; stakeholders should monitor regulatory developments for SPC procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: UPC court structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC consists of a Court of First Instance (divided into local, regional and central divisions), a Court of Appeal, and a Registry; there will also be a Patent Arbitration and Mediation Centre and a Training Centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of division affects procedure, language and possibly remedies; parties should consider which division is competent when planning litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central division technology allocation and seats
rubrics_metrics.description: The central division will have its seat in Paris with a section in Munich; the Paris seat will have competence for certain technologies (e.g., performing operations, textiles, software, electricity) and Munich for mechanical engineering and related fields; seats and sections determine competence for technology areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally London was to handle pharmaceuticals and life sciences, but following Brexit that seat is likely to be relocated (Milan mentioned as probable); until final decisions, cases may be distributed between Paris and Munich.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language of proceedings rules
rubrics_metrics.description: At first instance local and regional divisions will use the official language(s) of the hosting member state; the central division will use the language in which the patent was granted (English, French or German). The Court of Appeal follows the first instance language, with exceptions and party agreements possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a local/regional division provides a choice of language a claimant may choose; however, if the defendant only conducts activities in one member state with multiple official languages, the claimant must start in that region's language. Parties can agree exceptions; language choice affects evidence, pleadings and costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge qualifications and panel composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC will have legally qualified judges (qualified for appointment to judicial office in a contracting state) and technically qualified judges (university degree, proven expertise in a technological field, and knowledge of civil law and patent procedure). Each first instance case will be heard by three legally qualified judges (multinational composition); the Court of Appeal panels will sit with five judges (three legally qualified nationals of different states and two technically qualified judges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels are multinational; technically qualified judges bring technical expertise to appeal panels; language skills and patent litigation experience are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling infringement and validity together
rubrics_metrics.description: If infringement and a counterclaim for invalidity are brought before the central division, both will be dealt with together. Local/regional divisions may either proceed with both, refer the counterclaim to the central division (potential bifurcation), or refer both to the central division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bifurcation (separating infringement and validity) is possible and controversial; the practical effect may be limited but depends on division decisions. Appeals against separate decisions can be heard together by the Court of Appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional measures and available remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC can grant provisional measures including preliminary injunctions, seizure or delivery up of suspected infringing goods, precautionary seizure of movable and immovable property (including blocking bank accounts and other assets) and interim costs awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional measures are broad and can prevent entry or movement of goods in the channels of commerce; parties seeking urgent relief should be prepared to seek such measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with EPO opposition and accelerated proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties must inform the UPC of any pending EPO opposition proceedings and any requests for accelerated processing before the EPO; the UPC may request the EPO to accelerate or may stay UPC proceedings if a rapid EPO decision is expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic coordination between EPO oppositions and UPC litigation can affect timing and outcomes; the UPC has discretion to stay or request acceleration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected timeline for first instance decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: UPC litigation aims for first instance decisions on both infringement and validity (if in issue) within 12 to 14 months of proceedings being commenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an intended target to be quicker and cheaper than multiple national litigations; actual timing may vary by case complexity and division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to bring infringement claims (venue rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims for infringement, provisional/protective measures and injunctions, damages or compensation shall be brought before either the local or regional division in the member state where the actual or threatened infringement occurred, or where the defendant has residence or principal place of business (or in absence, place of business). If none apply or the member state has no local/regional division, proceedings will be before the central division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple divisions may be competent, providing some forum choice; choice of venue affects applicable language, remedies and tactical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to bring invalidity/revocation claims (venue rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims for revocation or declaration of non-infringement will normally be brought before the central division, unless an action for infringement of the same patent between the same parties has already been brought before a local or regional division, in which case these actions may only be brought before the same division again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local counterclaims for revocation may be: (a) proceeded with locally; (b) referred to central division; or (c) the whole case may be referred to central division with party agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenging venue and jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: A respondent may lodge a preliminary objection to the jurisdiction and competence of the UPC or division where the claim was brought within one month of service of the statement of claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness is strict (one month); preliminary objections are the mechanism to contest venue and competence early in the proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee standing and participation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: An exclusive licensee is entitled to bring actions before the UPC unless prohibited by the licence agreement; a non-exclusive licensee is only entitled if expressly permitted by the licence agreement. The patent proprietor must be given prior notice and may join the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A licensee cannot contest validity in an infringement action if the proprietor does not take part; to challenge validity the party must bring actions against the proprietor or secure their participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court fees: fixed and value-based fee structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Court fees include fixed fees and value-based fees. Infringement actions and declarations of non-infringement have fixed court fees of €11,000. Fixed fee for revocation actions is €20,000. Value-based fees apply to infringement/decl. non-infringement claims with value > €500,000: minimum value-based fee €2,500 (action value up to €750,000) up to maximum €325,000 (actions > €50m). Value-based fees do not apply to revocation actions or counterclaims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should budget for both fixed and potential value-based fees; the value thresholds and caps materially affect litigation economics for high-value disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recoverable legal costs and ceilings
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful party may recover reasonable and proportionate legal costs, subject to a ceiling based on claim value: maximum award of recoverable costs €2m for cases valued at more than €50m. The ceiling may be raised in particularly complex cases but cannot exceed €5m. The UPC may lower the ceiling on request if recoverable costs would threaten economic viability (e.g., universities, non-profits, public research organisations or natural persons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recoverable costs are capped but flexible in exceptional complexity or to protect vulnerable parties; parties should consider likely recoverable cost exposure when litigating.
